The global lock only protects cache state.\n        with refresh_lock:\n            with self._rule_cache_lock:\n                cached = self._fx_cache.get(pair)\n                if cached and (time.monotonic() - cached[1]) < self.cache_ttl:\n                    return cached[0]\n                stale = cached[0] if cached else None\n                backoff_until = self._fx_backoff_until.get(pair, 0.0)\n            if stale is not None and time.monotonic() < backoff_until:\n                return stale\n            try:\n                rate = self.fx_client.refresh_fx_quote(pair)\n            except FxUpstreamError:\n                if stale is None:\n                    raise\n                # Graceful degradation: keep serving the last good rate while\n                # upstream is returning 503. There's a subtle issue with single-flight + backoff during a 503 storm. The first thread fails after 0.9 seconds and sets the backoff. Threads that were waiting on refresh_lock then check the backoff → immediately return stale. Good. New threads check the backoff before acquiring refresh_lock → immediately return stale. So the worst-case P99 ≈ 0.9 seconds for just one thread per pair per 5-second window.\n\nBut actually — do we even need single-flight in the first place? It adds complexity. Without it, during a 503 storm with a stale cache: all threads with a stale cache miss do 0.9 seconds of retries in parallel (not serialized), then return stale. P99 ≈ 0.9 seconds for everyone, but no lock contention. With backoff, after the first failure everyone else is fast. Single-flight + backoff is strictly better, and it's not that complex.
